entries.title: Maren Haile-Selassie scores twice as Fire earn 4-4 draw at Toronto
entries.summary: <p>TORONTO — Derrick Etienne Jr. scored the tying goal in second-half stoppage time and Josh Sargent recorded his first career hat trick as Toronto FC rallied for a 4-4 draw against the Fire on Saturday night.</p><p>Toronto (5-7-11) allowed the first goal and came back to earn at least a draw for the eighth time this season.</p><p>Chicago (11-6-5) played to a draw for the third straight match.</p><p>Sargent scored his first goal on a strike from the center of the box in the 27th minute. Nine minutes later, Sargent sent a shot past Chicago goalkeeper Chris Brady for a 2-1 lead. Sargent broke a 2-all tie in the 54th for Toronto's first hat trick since Federico Bernardeschi did so against Montreal on May 18, 2024.</p><p>But a pair of defensive breakdowns led to Chicago reclaiming the lead.</p><p>Maren Haile-Selassie scored his second goal of the match for Chicago shortly after goalkeeper Luka Gavran made an initial save from distance but was caught out of position on the second chance.</p><p>Robert Lewandowski, who played his first professional match on Canadian soil, made it 4-3 Chicago in the 63rd.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Chicago: Hosts Miami on Wednesday.</p><p>Toronto: Stays home to play Nashville on Wednesday.</p>

entries.title: Suburban woman facing murder charges after killing 2-year-old before attempting self-harm
entries.summary: <p>A Frankfort woman is facing murder charges after she is alleged to have killed her 2-year-old son Tuesday, according to Will County prosecutors.</p><p>Corie Walsh, 40, is charged with three counts of first-degree murder, according to Will County prosecutors. </p><p>Walsh had reportedly recently become interested in the case of Lindsay Clancy, who was on trial in the deaths of her three children in January 2023. Walsh had been discussing the case in a group chat with friends three hours before her own child was found unresponsive, prosecutors said. </p><p>The case, which <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/live/lindsay-clancy-trial-09-04-2026" target="_blank" ><u>ended in a mistrial Friday</u></a>, has been live-streamed the last several weeks and drawn national attention.</p><p>Frankfort police responded to a call of an unresponsive child at Walsh’s home in the 22700 block of Brook Stone Court around 4 p.m. and found a neighbor performing CPR on a small child in the basement, prosecutors said. The neighbor said Barrett Walsh, 2, had been hanging from the rafters and was already without a pulse when he was discovered.</p><p>A medical examiner’s report determined the child died due to asphyxia, prosecutors said.</p><p>Police then found Walsh upstairs in a bathtub fully clothed and surrounded by bloody water, prosecutors said. The same neighbor said she had taken a knife from Walsh and held a cloth to the inside of Walsh’s leg where she had harmed herself.</p><p>Walsh reportedly told police her child was the “devil” and “anti-Christ,” and described to officers the way she had killed him, prosecutors said. </p><p>Prosecutors said Walsh explained she intended to harm her other children and husband when they returned home. Another infant in the home was not harmed. Walsh's two other children were away during the incident, and her husband was not in Illinois at the time.</p><p>Despite the rarity of the occurrences, there have been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/01/12/mothers-children-mental-health-drowning-stabbing-arson" target="_blank" ><u>several recent cases</u></a> in the Chicago area in which parents have harmed or killed their children.</p><p>In July 2025, Logan Square mother <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2025/07/06/woman-charged-fatal-stabbing-children-fire-logan-square" target="_blank" ><u>Wendy Tolbert</u></a> was similarly accused of killing her 4-year-old son and seriously injuring her two other children before attempting to burn down their home.</p><p>Tolbert had also said her children were “possessed by the devil” while admitting to police that she had harmed her children, according to prosecutors. She had previously struggled with mental health and recently been diagnosed with cancer. A date in her ongoing trial is set for next Wednesday.</p><p>Experts <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/01/12/mothers-children-mental-health-drowning-stabbing-arson" target="_blank" ><u>previously told the Sun-Times</u></a> that many injuries and deaths of children could have been prevented had more support — specifically mental health care — reached parents sooner.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/01/12/mothers-children-mental-health-drowning-stabbing-arson" >Stricken families search for answers after mothers are accused of harming children</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2025/07/06/woman-charged-fatal-stabbing-children-fire-logan-square" >Mom thought children were possessed by devil before stabbing them, prosecutors say</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Grayson Schmueck toughs it out to lead Payton past Amundsen
entries.summary: <p>One good arm was enough for Payton's Grayson Schmueck.</p><p>Schmueck contributed some productive runs and spearheaded a stingy defense as the Grizzlies grinded their way to a 13-12 win against Amundsen on a hot Saturday afternoon at Winnemac Stadium.</p><p>The senior ran 12 times for 69 yards — both game highs — with an arm that was wrapped and padded.</p><p>"Grayson is the heart and soul of the team," Payton quarterback Jackson Peters said. "He plays with 1000% effort. He has a sprained wrist right now in a club, and he said, 'I'm still going to play offense and defense without having to stop. Yeah ... we rally behind guys like him who want to play 100% effort every play."</p><p>That's a necessity given his size, according to Schmueck.</p><p>"Really, [I'm] just doing anything I can," he said. "I mean, I'm 165 pounds playing at a linebacker. It's not a great recipe. But I'm out here making plays and stuff, just doing anything I can."</p><p>How does he carry the ball with the injury?</p><p>"I mean, just go right hand and use [the club] to whack some people," he said with a smile.</p><p>In any case, Schmueck has done enough to help Payton (3-0) continue its push for a 15th consecutive IHSA playoff berth. The leaders of last year's 7-3 team, two-way stars Thomas Fitchett and Sam Merrill, have graduated and Schmueck and Peters have stepped up to replace them.</p><p>"He's a slot guy, he's a do-everything [player]," Payton coach Calvin Clark said of Schmueck. "That kid said, 'Give me the ball, coach.'</p><p>"And you've got to love this game with guys like him, man. ... I'm not the coach I am without a Grayson at the end of the day."</p><p>Peters has been clutch as well. He accounted for both Payton touchdowns on Saturday, throwing a nine-yard TD pass to Israel Oluwalana in the second quarter and running six yards for the go-ahead score with 3:31 left in the game. Peters was 8-of-14 passing for 99 yards with no interceptions.</p><p>Peters went 3-0 as the Grizzlies' starting quarterback last season before Fitchett took over as the No. 1.</p><p>"So he has leadership already," Clark said. "And he's just built to be an outstanding and great quarterback.</p><p>"You saw it in that last drive. I looked at him when we went down, and the team didn't get down. We knew this is what we work hard for during practice."</p><p>Amundsen (1-2) is in a transition year after graduating 20 starters. One of the two returning regulars is junior quarterback Jake Siefert, who played receiver last season.</p><p>He completed 12 of 23 passes for 139 yards with no interceptions and ran seven times for 50 yards. His 12-yard TD run with 7:33 left gave the Vikings a 12-7 lead. Milton Follmar also had a short TD run for Amundsen.</p><p>"We're a very young team and I told my coaches we've got to stay positive with them," Vikings coach Nick Olson said. "... [Payton's] kids just wanted it more today, And they were disciplined and we weren't disciplined. We need to continue to work on majoring in the minors and figuring out the small nuances in the game of football."</p>

entries.title: Lincoln-Way East students accused of racial harassment at Homewood-Flossmoor football game
entries.summary: <p>Police removed multiple people from the Lincoln-Way East student section in the third quarter of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/04/lincoln-way-east-football-homewood-flossmoor" >Friday’s game between visiting Lincoln-Way East and Homewood-Flossmoor in Flossmoor</a>. </p><p>The teams, most fans and media were unaware of what had happened, but photos and videos began appearing on social media on Saturday morning. Later on Saturday, both schools addressed the incident. </p><p>According to a statement from H-F superintendent Jennifer Norrell and principal Clinton Alexander, "five Lincoln-Way East student fans made a very bad choice to engage in disrespectful and racist harassment towards H-F students seated in the bleachers."</p><p>Alexander was at the game. The statement goes on to say that H-F is working with Lincoln-Way East and local authorities "as we consider all options to protect against this in the future, including legal options."</p><p>Lincoln-Way East released the following statement:</p><p>"We are aware that a group of five Lincoln-Way East students displayed inappropriate and offensive behavior at the football game against Homewood-Flossmoor on Friday night. The students involved are not members of the football team. We would like to sincerely apologize to the HF community for the behavior displayed by these students. This behavior does not reflect the expectations and standards we have for Lincoln-Way students.</p><p>The district is taking this matter seriously. We have identified the students involved and will follow through with the district's discipline policies and procedures to the fullest extent.</p><p>Because this matter involves students, we cannot disclose the names of those involved or the disciplinary action that is to be taken."</p><p>Homewood-Flossmoor plans to address the matter with its entire student body this week. </p><p>"We as an H-F Community are an example for how to live and thrive as a community of diverse individuals," Homewood-Flossmoor's statement said. "We want to remain the model and also a model for how we respond to those who attempt to disrespect and ultimately distract us from our goals."</p>

entries.title: Can Alex Bregman add to his, Cubs’ Gold Glove haul? ‘This has got to be one of his best seasons defensively’
entries.summary: <p>MIAMI – <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> is perhaps the best defender in baseball, and he showed why in Friday’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> win over the Marlins, making an outstanding leaping catch at the center-field wall.</p><p>A few days earlier, it was second baseman <b>Nico Hoerner</b> – <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/04/cubs-nico-hoerner-dansby-swanson-shortstop-gold-glove-best-defense-in-baseball-oblique-injury" >playing shortstop with <b>Dansby Swanson</b> on the IL</a> – making a highlight-reel diving catch against the Brewers.</p><p>The Cubs are baseball’s best defensive team, but with all the web gems Crow-Armstrong and Hoerner and Swanson turn in on such a regular basis, someone is perhaps getting lost in the shuffle.</p><p>“Breggy’s been outright Gold Glove caliber at third,” Crow-Armstrong said Thursday.</p><p>Yes, <b>Alex Bregman</b>’s bat is not the only thing the third baseman is impressing with right now. He’s played spectacular defense at the hot corner for much of the campaign, in line with all the other sparkling glovework around the diamond for this Cubs team.</p><p>“Alex has had a quietly excellent defensive season,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said Saturday. “When you’re playing on a defense with Pete and <b>Ian [Happ]</b> and Dansby and Nico, it’s hard to talk about everybody. But Alex, the first two weeks of the year, he probably didn’t like, and then since then, he’s been really incredible.</p><p>“He’s played a Gold Glove level third base, I think.”</p><p>Make it two votes, then, for a Gold Glove.</p><p>“He’s made hard plays. He’s made every routine play. He’s thrown very accurately,” Counsell said. “I haven’t seen previous Alex Bregman seasons, necessarily, daily, but this has got to be one of his best seasons defensively.”</p><p>This wouldn’t be a first. Bregman won a Gold Glove during his final year with the Astros in 2024.</p><p>But Counsell’s suggestion that this might be the best season the 11-year major league veteran has had is backed up by defensive metrics. In fact, according to some of those numbers, it’s far and away the best defensive season Bregman’s had in the big leagues.</p><p>He started Saturday with 13 Defensive Runs Saved, a career high that’s more than double the mark he posted during his Gold Glove campaign in 2024, when he had six in that department.</p><p>He came into Saturday with seven Outs Above Average and a Fielding Run Value of six, figures bested only once previously in his career, in his hardware-winning season of 2024.</p><p>This is a Cubs team built on defense, and <b>Jed Hoyer</b>’s front office stuck to that script when it spent big on Bregman last winter.</p><p>If this group is going to achieve its ultimate goal, it’ll be by getting the type of plays Bregman & Co. have made all season long, perhaps earning them another trophy case full of Gold Gloves.</p><p><b>Z saves the day</b></p><p>The Cubs never trailed the Marlins in Saturday’s 6-5 win, but it was a bumpy ride for the bullpen, which allowed two homers.</p><p>Righty <b>Ryan Zeferjahn</b>, though, shut the door with a five-out save.</p><p>After posting a 7.20 ERA through his first 11 outings as a Cub, he’s been near perfect in his last two.</p><p>“Even when I was still struggling, toward the end of that struggle, the process was still there for me,” Zeferjahn said after the game. “Everything was working, just sometimes results weren’t there. We stayed on course with that, and we’re going to keep doing that, keep hammering that home.</p><p>“Hopefully, we stay on this roll.”</p><p><b>Assad returns</b></p><p>The Cubs brought righty <b>Javier Assad</b> up from Triple-A to start Saturday, seeing an opportunity in the final weeks of the regular season to get an extra day of rest for their starters.</p><p>Assad struggled a bit Saturday, walking a season-high five batters.</p>

entries.title: Rogers Park police pursuit of reported stolen vehicle ends in CPD officers, pedestrian injured
entries.summary: <p>A police pursuit of a suspected stolen vehicle in Rogers Park ended with an injured pedestrian and two officers on Friday evening. </p><p>Chicago police officers reportedly noticed a red Toyota matching the description of a stolen vehicle at 7:14 p.m. in Rogers Park, officials said. </p><p>The officers tried to initiate a traffic stop in the 2000 block of W. Birchwood Ave., but the driver of the sedan, an unidentified 25-year-old man, did not stop and eventually struck the police vehicle during the chase, police said.</p><p>Shortly after, the sedan hit a light-colored Volkswagen SUV in the 7400 block of North Sheridan Road.</p><p>The Volkswagen SUV then struck a 24-year-old man who had been walking on a nearby sidewalk, police said. He was taken to the hospital in fair condition and treated for injuries.</p><p>Following the crash, the driver and a passenger of the suspected stolen sedan were taken into custody. The driver sustained "unknown injuries," police said, and was taken to Swedish Covenant Hospital in good condition. </p><p>During the chase, two CPD officers were injured. They were taken to an area hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, police said. </p><p>Charges are pending as of Saturday evening.</p>

entries.title: Northwestern's defense bends but doesnt break in season-opening win
entries.summary: <p>Aidan Chiles threw for 273 yards and a touchdown in his debut, and Northwestern pulled away late to top FCS South Dakota State 34-18 on Saturday night at Martin Stadium in Evanston.</p><p>Chiles, who made 20 starts for Michigan State before joining the Wildcats during the offseason, made it a two-possession game with a 14-yard draw-play touchdown with 4:34 to go.</p><p>South Dakota State’s (1-1) Josiah Johnson scored with 8:16 left to cut the lead to 20-18, but a two-point try failed. Northwestern took the kickoff and burned off almost four minutes before Chiles scored.</p><p>“We got where we needed to get and did what we needed to do at the end,” Chiles said.</p><p>Joseph Himon II (four carries, 87 yards) took off for an 80-yard touchdown run with 1:14 left to widen the final score.</p><p>The Wildcats’ defense gave up 438 yards but kept the Jackrabbits out of the end zone on six of seven trips inside their 25-yard line.</p><p>“I thought we came up with a great plan and executed it well,” Northwestern coach David Braun said. “We found a way not to break, and that was the difference in the game.”</p><p>Chiles hit Griffin Wilde with a 71-yard pass on his first play from scrimmage, then found Alex Honing with an 11-yard touchdown pass less than four minutes into the game to give the hosts a lead they never lost.</p><p>Caleb Komolafe had a short touchdown run midway through the third quarter for the Wildcats, who’ve won four straight home openers.</p><p>Chase Mason was 23 for 48 for 285 yards with an interception for the Jackrabbits. Johnson had 79 yards on 19 carries and Tristan Alvano had four field goals.</p><p>South Dakota State drove deep into Northwestern territory twice in the second quarter but had to settle for a pair of Alvano field goals and trailed 10-6 at intermission.</p><p>“Too many missed opportunities,” Jackrabbits coach Dan Jackson said. “I thought we had opportunities to really punch some things in when we had the ball in the red zone and make a statement, but we didn’t do it.”</p><p><b>The Takeaway</b></p><p>South Dakota State: Give Northwestern’s defense credit, but the Jackrabbits had seven drives deep into the hosts’ territory but came away with just one touchdown. The loss left the program 2-12 against FBS opponents.</p><p>Northwestern: Former Oregon and NFL coach Chip Kelly is the new offensive coordinator, and his unit amassed almost 500 yards Saturday night. The Wildcats have just one more game to keep fine-tuning before a Sept. 25 trip to reigning national champion Indiana.</p><p><b>Scary Moment</b></p><p>The game was delayed several minutes early in the third quarter after Northwestern offensive lineman Jackson Carsello appeared to take a teammate’s knee to his helmet at the end of a play. The 6-4, 300-pound Carsello was fitted with a head-and-neck stabilizer and placed on a stretcher, but appeared conscious and repeatedly gave a thumbs-up sign as he was taken off the field.</p><p>Braun did not update Carsello’s condition after the game, but said the player was in “good spirits.”</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>The Jackrabbits host New Haven on Sept. 12.</p><p>The Wildcats get an early bye next weekend and welcome Colorado on Sept. 19.</p>

entries.title: Anthony Kay again can't get through fifth inning as White Sox fall to Twins
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox’ relief corps continues to lead the majors in innings pitched, and at the rate the starters are going, the relievers should win in a runaway.</p><p>That’s not a good thing.</p><p>Left-hander Anthony Kay allowed five runs in 4 ⅓ innings Saturday in the Sox’ 6-4 loss to the Twins, his third consecutive start with fewer than five innings. It extended the rotation’s failure to reach six innings to 14 consecutive games. The Sox have weathered their starters’ inability to pitch deep into games this long, but you have to wonder how much longer they can.</p><p>The Sox gave Kay a 3-0 lead in the first on a two-run homer by Munetaka Murakami, his 30th of the season, and a solo shot by Colson Montgomery, his 31st. But after pitching three hitless innings, Kay began to unravel, the big blow coming on Ryan Jeffers’ three-run homer in the fifth, a 415-foot shot to left field.</p><p>“We got in a groove early and then kind of fell apart,” Kay said. “Second and third time around, they pick up good swings. It comes down to execution and maybe some pitch-calling that we can work on second time, third time through. They’re clearly seeing something that we have to work on.”</p><p>“You have to find ways to get outs and get through the fifth there,” manager Will Venable said. “Obviously, it’s been something that we’ve been struggling with as a staff. You’re in a spot going into that inning, I think 62-63 pitches, and you want to be able to push through. Just some pitches left over the middle of the plate.”</p><p>The last Sox starter to pitch six innings was Sean Burke on Aug. 21. It hasn’t happened nearly enough, and the Sox have to hope that an overworked bullpen doesn’t come back to bite them in the final 20 games of the season.</p><p>“You’re going to expose guys to some spots like we did today in the fifth with Kay facing [right-handed-hitting] Jeffers where you’re going to have some trouble you’ve got to be able to work through," Venable said. </p><h3>Rotation roulette</h3><p>Venable changed the Sox’ rotation, taking advantage of the team’s day off Monday. He moved Sean Burke from Sunday in the series finale against the Twins to Tuesday in the opener against the Pirates. Bryan Hudson will be the opener for a bullpen day Sunday.</p><p>“[We] have a chance to line some things up,” Venable said. “We’re looking ahead and trying to get guys in the best spots. There’s some implications with rest; there’s some implications with matchups.”</p><p>Burke is more than 20 innings past his career high and probably could use the extra two days of rest. He’s coming off one of his better starts of late in which he pitched 5 ⅔ scoreless innings of one-hit ball against the Astros, though he walked four.</p><p>“We’ve seen him so good,” Venable said. “Feel like he’s getting back to form after a couple that maybe weren’t as sharp as the previous stretch. Feel really good about where he’s at and want to make sure that he stays there.”</p><p>Burke will be followed by Davis Martin on Wednesday and a starter to be announced for Thursday. Based on the last run through the rotation, that would be Luis Castillo’s turn. But since his seven scoreless innings Aug. 12 against the Reds, his ERA is 9.98 in four starts.</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>Catcher Kyle Teel felt good after his first game back from injury Friday. Teel, who missed six weeks with a sprained ankle, didn’t start Saturday — he struck out as a pinch hitter in the seventh and stayed in the game — but is expected to Sunday.</p><p>“I thought he played at a really good pace, especially for his first game back,” Venable said. “I know there were emotions and some excitement. But he was really calm, really did a nice job being in tune with what he needed to do out there.”</p><p>• Winston-Salem outfielder George Wolkow, 20, became the youngest Sox minor-leaguer since at least 1981 (Adam Grundt) to reach 100 RBI in a season. entries.title: Boy, 15, found with gunshot wounds in South Shore
entries.summary: <p>A 15-year-old was shot multiple times on Saturday in South Shore, Chicago police said. </p><p>Police at about 8:07 p.m. responded to the 6800 block of South Dorchester Avenue and discovered the teenage boy with multiple gunshot wounds to the leg and buttocks, according to police.</p><p>The boy was taken to Comer Children’s Hospital in good condition, police said.</p><p>Area detectives are investigating the shooting. </p>

entries.title: Do Blackhawks have a path to fourth place in Central Division?
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> are going to talk a lot about competing for the playoffs this season.</p><p>Defenseman Alex Vlasic has led the way with that rhetoric, hoping to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/08/23/blackhawks-alex-vlasic-playoffs-louis-crevier-bowen-byram-patrick-kane" target="_blank" >speak it into existence</a>, but he won’t be alone once his teammates start doing regular interviews during training camp, which starts Sept. 17.</p><p>What would it take for the Hawks to make the playoffs? It certainly sounds unlikely, given how far outside the field the Hawks have been recently. They missed by 18 points last season, by 35 the season before and by a whopping 46 the season before that.</p><p>The influx of talented youth in the last couple of years, forward Patrick Kane’s return and defenseman Bowen Byram’s arrival this summer make this clearly the best Hawks roster under general manager Kyle Davidson. But that’s not saying much. Jumping over so many competitors to get into the postseason will be no easy feat.</p><p>Unsurprisingly, the analytics models and betting lines are skeptical. The Hawks’ playoff odds are +400 on FanDuel, for example, which equates to a 20% implied probability — the third-lowest odds in the Western Conference.</p><p>The Hawks’ internal target needs to be fourth place in the intimidating Central Division, which likely would earn them a wild-card spot, given how weak the Pacific Division is. Even fifth in the Central might be enough, but fourth is a safer target.</p><p>And if you don multiple pairs of rose-tinted glasses and squint, fourth in the Central seems somewhat within the realm of possibility.</p><p>Third? Not so much. The Avalanche, Wild and Stars were by far the best teams in the division and in the conference last season, and they’re expected to remain the class of the division (at least) again this season.</p><p>Off the ice, the Wild and Stars have the looming 2027 free agencies of Quinn Hughes and Jason Robertson to worry about, but their rosters are elite for now. The Avalanche, meanwhile, changed little this summer after their 121-point season.</p><p>The rest of the division appears to be less superhuman. The Mammoth, Predators, Blues and Jets have flaws. They’re all projected to finish above the Hawks, of course, but it’s not inconceivable the Hawks could leapfrog them if a number of things break right.</p><p>For reference, here are DraftKings’ current point-total over/under lines for each Central team: Avalanche, 107.5; Wild, 101.5; Stars, 100.5; Mammoth, 96.5; Predators, 85.5; Blues, 84.5; Jets, 84.5; Hawks 79.5.</p><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Erin Hooley/AP file photo</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Looking around</b></h3><p>Center Connor Bedard most often gets compared to peers such as Macklin Celebrini and Leo Carlsson for obvious reasons, but he’s friends with Celebrini and respectful with Carlsson.</p><p>It’s actually young Mammoth star Logan Cooley with whom Bedard seems perhaps most eager to create a rivalry. He had great success on that front last season, as the Hawks swept the four-game season series from the Mammoth.</p><p>‘‘Every game we play [against] these guys is pretty intense and pretty good hockey, so it feels great to beat them every time,’’ Bedard said in March. ‘‘We don’t like them; they don’t like us. So it’s a good feeling.’’</p><p>Cooley, Dylan Guenther and Clayton Keller form a dangerous three-headed monster atop the Mammoth’s forward corps, which was bolstered this summer by veterans Vincent Trocheck and Anders Lee. A top-tier prospect pool lies beneath the Mammoth’s solid NHL roster, so the future is undeniably bright in Salt Lake City.</p><p>For the Hawks to surpass them this season — and keep pace in the long term — they’ll need to keep channeling that emotional fire. Talent matters, but so does willpower. They probably also will need goalie Spencer Knight to outperform Mammoth veteran Karel Vejmelka and pan out better than Mammoth goalie prospects Sebastian Cossa and Michael Hrabal.</p><p>Speaking of Central goalies, Connor Hellebuyck’s decision to go public with his trade request out of Winnipeg throws the Jets into crisis mode because they would be obvious pretenders without him.</p><p>It’s no coincidence the Jets won the Presidents’ Trophy in 2024-25, when Hellebuyck posted a .925 save percentage, then fell out of the playoffs entirely in 2025-26, when he posted an .895 save percentage.</p><p>Yes, Kyle Connor and Josh Morrissey are great players, but it’s never good when a franchise that can’t attract free-agent talent also has one of the worst prospect pools.</p><p>Even if the Jets keep Hellebuyck, who still has five years left under contract, the Hawks have much better center depth and conceivably could find a way to score their way past them. If the Jets trade Hellebuyck, the Hawks might move above them even in the preseason betting lines.</p><p>That leaves the Predators and Blues, who finished last season tied with 86 points. Given the Predators’ Juuse Saros has declined for three consecutive seasons and the Blues’ Jordan Binnington is coming off a disastrous season, neither goalie situation is airtight, either.</p><p>Both franchises’ new GMs, Chris MacFarland (Predators) and Alexander Steen (Blues), spent their summers moving around lots of forward deck chairs.</p><p>In Nashville, Mavrik Bourque, Ross Colton, Jack Drury and others replace Luke Evangelista, Erik Haula and Fedor Svechkov. In St. Louis, Mason McTavish and Connor McMichael replace Jordan Kryou and Jonathan Drouin.</p><p>On the whole, the Predators’ extremely old roster looks worse than the Blues’ decent collection of young and prime-aged talent.</p><p>In the long term, one Hawks concern might be that their prospect pool is only marginally better than the Predators’ and Blues’ pools, which are strong. This season, the Hawks’ best chance of surpassing their Midwestern neighbors might depend on their defense.</p><p>The Predators rely heavily on two defensemen in their mid-30s (Roman Josi and Brady Skjei). The Blues, aside from Philip Broberg, do nearly the same with Colton Parayko and Cam Fowler. If Artyom Levshunov and Sam Rinzel break out and Byram emerges as the No. 1 defenseman the Hawks are paying him to be, the scales might tip favorably.</p><h3>Wait and see</h3><p>The Hawks themselves, it’s worth noting, won’t pay much attention to these opponent-by-opponent matchups until the specific games arrive on their schedule.</p><p>They’re at the stage of rebuilding where they must focus on bettering themselves and let the standings fall where they may.</p><p>Looking down from above, however, the Hawks’ loftier ambitions this season require a little more focus on their division rivals. If things go well, this might be the first season in some time in which the NHL standings actually matter to them for more than determining draft position.</p><p>The Hawks will face the Mammoth in their second game, the Blues in their fourth (their home opener) and the Jets in their eighth, providing some early referendums — albeit without Bedard in the lineup.</p><p>Then they’ll finish the season facing the Predators three times in their last eight games, a weird scheduling quirk. By then, it should be clear whether Vlasic and his cohorts’ proclamations about the playoffs were prescient or foolish.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Antisocial husband ruins all the fun
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I have been married for eight years. For the most part, we are happy, but there is one thing that upsets me. He doesn't like to have people over for social events. In fact, I can't get him to participate in any social outing without him moaning and complaining the entire time.</p><p>I enjoy getting together with friends and having people over and so do our children. I love hosting birthday parties, barbecues and such, and I would love to have couples over for drinks or even a game night. It's a constant struggle because my husband won't meet me halfway. I feel like I'm trapped in my own home and can't go anywhere. If I do go, he rarely accompanies me and our kids to social gatherings, and I am left to explain why he isn't with us. I hate being put in this position. How can I make him meet me halfway? — <i>HELD BACK</i></p><p><b>DEAR HELD BACK:</b> Short of ordering your husband to socialize at gunpoint, there's nothing you can do. (Please do not point a gun at your husband.) By now, you should have realized that you can't change him. You can, however, change how you react to his behavior.</p><p>Unless he had a complete personality change after the wedding, this is the person you married. Because this is who he is, it's up to you to be less embarrassed and more up-front about explaining his absence when you and your children socialize without him. ("You know, 'Harry' just isn't comfortable socializing. It's not in his nature.")</p><p>Unless he forbids you to host a game night once in a while, go ahead and plan one. If he's as antisocial as you say he is, he won't be missed.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My granddaughter "Carrie" is getting married this fall. She has asked me to escort her down the aisle. She is in her mid-30s, and this is her second marriage. I am honored but also uncomfortable. Her mother (my daughter, "Lori") and father were never married, and they have three children together. He was emotionally and physically abusive to the children and my daughter.</p><p>Carrie is estranged from her father and has had nothing to do with him for several years. She is also estranged from her mother. She feels that Lori has never been a mother to her, didn't protect her or her siblings from their father and has recently made little effort to show an interest in her life.</p><p>I have not yet told Lori that Carrie asked me to escort her down the aisle. I know Lori will be heartbroken. I am afraid that when I do tell her, our relationship will suffer. It is a long time between now and the wedding. Any suggestions? — <i>CONFLICTED GRANDMOTHER</i></p><p><b>DEAR GRANDMOTHER:</b> Lori must already know that she won't be invited to the ceremony, much less be a member of the wedding party. She can't expect Carrie to walk down the aisle alone, so I hope she will be grateful that Carrie has a proud grandmother to fill the role. If not, that's her problem; do not make it yours. Help give Carrie a loving, happy wedding day, and don't allow the conflict between them to drag you down.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: The Peggy Notebaert Nature Museum’s sendoff party for monarch butterflies
entries.summary: <p>In a room transformed into a lush forest, a dad knelt beside his nervous daughter, gently reassuring her.</p><p>"I know this may be scary, but these butterflies aren’t dangerous,” he explained. “They just want to spread their wings and fly.”</p><p>The Peggy Notebaert Nature Museum hosted its annual Flutter into Fall event Saturday, celebrating monarch butterflies as they prepare for their journey south to Mexico. Children and adults learned about the monarch’s migration patterns, enjoyed arts and crafts, took in cultural performances and watched butterflies be released into the sky.</p><p>“Education of people is important for the betterment of our environment, and that helps these species,” said Jeffery Wolfthal, public programs manager at the Nature Museum. “The more you understand and appreciate entries.title: Craig Counsell or Pat Murphy? We went to Whitefish Bay for the answer
entries.summary: <p>WHITEFISH BAY, Wis. — Not sure if you knew this, but Brewers manager Pat Murphy invented bratwurst.</p><p>And beer. And Friday fish fries. And supper clubs. And Brandy Old-Fashioneds. Not to mention cheesehead hats and deer stands.</p><p>All that might as well be true, anyway, as much as Wisconsin loves the 67-year-old skipper, who has a real chance at a third straight National League manager of the year award.</p><p>Murphy’s predecessor, Craig Counsell, never won one of those. That’s because Counsell is a no-good bum. Don’t let his three division titles and five playoff appearances as Brewers manager — or his third straight winning season and soon-to-be second straight playoff trip with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> — fool you.</p><p>Brewers fans still love to boo and rip the winningest manager in team history, who happens to have grown up here, played here, ushered in a winning era here and continued to live here, a mere 10 miles from American Family Field.</p><p>Starting Monday, the Cubs are back in Milwaukee for the first time since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/28/chicago-cubs-milwaukee-brewers-craig-counsell-pete-crow-armstrong-dansby-swanson" target="_blank" >winning a key series against the Brewers in late June</a>. In the rubber match, a 4-3 win in 10 innings, Counsell used seven pitchers, pulling all the right levers as the suddenly soaring Cubs raised their record to 12-4 following a brutal 5-18 stretch. The Brewers still led the Cubs by 5½ games, but it looked like the division race could be hotter than butter-burger grease the rest of the way.</p><p>It gave me an idea: Why not spend a day in Counsell’s beloved stomping grounds — Whitefish Bay — to see if there was one place in Brewerland where fans still rated the manager with 707 Brewers wins ahead of his former bench coach, who at the time had 467 fewer of them?</p><p>My first stop was the office of Whitefish Bay High School athletic director Randee Drew, who has witnessed the athletic exploits of all four of Counsell’s children at the school where their old man, now 56, roamed the diamond ages before leaving the Brewers behind for the Cubs.</p><p>“Just a great family and a very supportive, popular dad,” Drew said. “He comes to everything. In my opinion, he’s very humble. If we were all blessed with the opportunities that Mr. Counsell has created for himself, I think a lot of people would make similar choices. If people knew him, they would know how great of a person he is.”</p><p>Counsell over Murphy, then?</p><p>“Oh, I’m not going to answer that,” Drew said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/HXeis_2ydEU?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Brewers fans from Whitefish Bay decide: Pat Murphy or Craig Counsell?"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Across the hall, the gym was bustling with summer activity. At the top of a stairway from the basketball court to the weight room, I found Counsell’s retired No. 19 jersey framed in glass. A couple of dozen Dukes were hard at work, which I took as an invitation to rudely interrupt everything.</p><p>Murphy or Counsell? Let’s just say I might have been pointing to a certain jersey for effect.</p><p>“Murphy,” the three who took note of a lumbering interloper replied.</p><p>Even here, in Counsell’s school?</p><p>“Doesn’t matter,” said both Charlie and Owen, sophomore baseball players.</p><p>“You can’t be a Brewers manager and then dip and head to the Cubs,” said Cal, a junior soccer player and golfer.</p><p>All agreed Murphy’s Brewers again would rule the roost in the National League Central when all was said and done.</p><p>I tried Sendik’s grocery store, stopping at the meat counter.</p><p>“Can I help you with anything?” a man asked.</p><p>Yes. Better Brewers manager, Counsell or Murphy?</p><p>“You need to talk to Joe.”</p><p>In produce, I found Joseph Galioto, 69, a diehard fan since the Brewers moved to Milwaukee in 1970. Counsell has been shopping here since way back when, turns out.</p><p>“Yeah, I’m good friends with him,” Galioto said.</p><p>Ah — this must be one strong vote for the pride of Whitefish.</p><p>“I pick Murphy,” Galioto said. “Murphy lets them do what they want — bunt, sacrifice, steal — on their own. … When [Counsell] was managing the Brewers, he didn’t know how to bunt. And Murphy lets the pitchers pitch.”</p><p>Next: the village’s Little League home, named for a certain highly accomplished skipper. No, not Murphy, for God’s sake.</p><p>At Craig Counsell Park — the man’s name is on the signs and everything — there could be only one numero uno. No games were happening on this day, but Joe Wollersheim, 43, was stocking the concession stand he runs.</p><p>Counsell over Murphy?</p><p>“Uh, absolutely not,” Wollersheim said. “I can’t call it ‘Craig Counsell Park’ anymore. I just call it ‘CCP.’ ”</p><p>But this was a baseball question, after all, not a popularity contest.</p><p>“I appreciate what baseball is trying to do with analytics, but I much appreciate Murph being old school, a gut-feeling guy,” said Wollersheim, who rates himself a 10 as a fan on a 1-10 scale. “He just seems like he shows emotion. The more distance from Counsell, the more I don’t like his managing style. He doesn’t seem like he’s as good with people.”</p><p>Harsh. The situation called for one of a veteran reporter’s go-to moves.</p><p>I bellied up to the bar at The Bay and ordered a cold one.</p><p>Seated next to me was Erin Byrne, 54, who lives up this way and prefers the Brewers but also did stints in Lincoln Park, Roscoe Village and Evanston and has a soft spot for the Cubs — and for Counsell.</p><p>“I used to see him at a deli, just a neighborhood deli, and it was a nice thing to see,” Byrne said. “He was very friendly. Right here in the neighborhood.”</p><p>Though I wasn’t sure I should bother, I had to ask.</p><p>Counsell or the other flippin’ guy?</p><p>“I will admit I don’t know a ton about baseball,” she said, “but I will say Craig Counsell.”</p><p>Maybe, just maybe, she knows more than she thinks.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel entries.title: Teen shot in Chicago Lawn drive-by shooting
entries.summary: <p>A 16-year-old boy was injured in a drive-by shooting late Saturday in the Chicago Lawn neighborhood, Chicago police said.</p><p>The boy was walking in the 6400 block of South Claremont Avenue when a dark SUV drove past and someone inside shot him in his leg around 11 p.m., according to police. He was taken in stable condition to Holy Cross Hospital.</p><p>No one has been arrested, police said.</p><p>Another <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/09/05/boy-15-found-with-gunshot-wounds-in-south-shore" target="_blank" >teenage boy was shot</a> just three hours earlier in South Shore.<br></p>

entries.title: Woman found fatally shot in Near West Side home
entries.summary: <p>A 42-year-old woman was found fatally shot inside a Near West Side home at around midnight Saturday, Chicago police said.</p><p>Officers discovered the woman, who has not been identified, inside the home in the 2100 block of West Jackson Boulevard. She was shot several times and was taken to Stroger Hospital where she was pronounced dead, according to police.</p><p>No one has been arrested, police said.</p>

entries.title: Is the Bulls' Matas Buzelis almost a forgotten man? It feels that way
entries.summary: <p>It seems as though Matas Buzelis suddenly has become the forgotten man on the Bulls’ roster.</p><p>Heck, NBA 2K27 didn’t even show the multitalented forward his due respect, giving him an 81 ranking on the latest version of the gaming franchise. That puts him in the same territory as Onyeka Okongwu, Walker Kessler and Devin Vassell.</p><p>At last look, however, Okongwu, Kessler and Vassell didn’t join the list of players with at least 170 three-pointers and 115 blocked shots in the same season in 2025-26. Nope, that was Buzelis who moved into that exclusive neighborhood, which also features Dirk Nowitzki, Kevin Durant, Rasheed Wallace, Brook Lopez and Myles Turner. Buzelis is the youngest of that group to do it.</p><p>Not bad for someone in the second season of his NBA career and who turned 21 last October.</p><p>The offseason hype surrounding the Bulls, however, is about rookie Caleb Wilson, new coach Tiago Splitter, a new front office led by Bryson Graham and even the addition of free-agent guard Norman Powell, who is coming off his first All-Star season.</p><p>Just a little reminder that Buzelis said at the end of last season that he was going to continue chasing greatness and showing the Bulls he can be a winning player.</p><p>‘‘I know this summer I am going to work my butt off,’’ Buzelis said in his exit interview with the media in April. ‘‘The whole summer, it’s going to be a hard summer for me. Getting my body stronger and sharpening pretty much everything. But mainly the body part, the shot, the handle, just everything. The main thing will be [adding] the strength.’’</p><p>He already was checking those boxes in late July, when he showed up to Las Vegas to watch Summer League play and looked stronger.</p><p>‘‘I always want more for myself and the team,’’ Buzelis said. ‘‘I definitely believe that I am [a foundation piece]. I know for a fact I am only going to get better. If they want me here and they believe in me, I’m here. I believe I am definitely a big piece, and I am going to continue to work and put my head down and grind to show it.’’</p><p>And what a time for him to show it, with Buzelis having a new-look frontcourt that might play to his strengths even more.</p><p>The additions of Nic Claxton and Wilson not only will give Buzelis more help protecting the rim, they also will allow him to play either forward spot, taking advantage of his versatility.</p><p>There were times in Summer League play that Wilson looked capable of playing small forward, but Buzelis showed it at the NBA level last season. According to Basketball Index, he was in the 72nd percentile in matchup difficulty and in the 84th percentile in perimeter isolation defense.</p><p>That shows Buzelis can develop into an elite two-way player who can protect the rim at an elite level but also switch to any player and be a force on the perimeter.</p><p>If Wilson’s skills translate to NBA basketball — which they should — and Claxton’s back issues are behind him, Splitter will have a frontcourt that has the potential to make life difficult for opponents in the paint and on the perimeter alike.</p><p>Buzelis will be a major reason why.</p><p>Remember him?</p>
